signals.text: Builds things outside the syllabus and can show them: personal projects with an up-to-date portfolio or GitHub link.

sources.quote: You may already have some personal experience from working on your own projects, which could be of interest to potential employers.
If you include a link to a portfolio, make sure it includes up-to-date examples of your work.

signals.text: Visible 'passion for technology': hackathons, tech events and self-started projects.

sources.quote: Recruiters have told targetjobs that they really want to see practical examples of candidates’ skills and demonstrations of candidates’ ‘passion for technology’
Software engineers are typically passionate about what they do and may already have a portfolio or some examples to show to potential employers

signals.text: Can talk in depth about their own projects: technology choices, trade-offs and what they would change.

sources.quote: Be prepared to talk in depth about projects you’ve worked on recently. Your interviewer will want to hear about technology choices, trade-offs
you need to be prepared to speak about anything on your CV at interview.

signals.text: Collaboration and communication count as much as technical skill.

sources.quote: the collaboration and project delivery skills we explore in this stage are just as important as technical excellence.
employers view behavioural competencies and ‘soft’ skills with equal importance.
the ability to communicate with clients, colleagues, and management to explain complex issues clearly and concisely

signals.text: Problem-solving ability is a core requirement; Monzo says it hires for problem-solving ability over experience.

sources.quote: In general, we hire for problem-solving ability over experience.
a logical, analytical and creative approach to problems and problem solving

signals.text: Skills are applied and self-driven, not just listed.
signals.basis: evidence (employer recruiter quoted by careers publisher + careers publisher)

sources.quote: Don’t just say, “I know programming languages x, y and z” – that doesn’t show passion and doesn’t stand out.
a motivated approach to your career and a willingness to further develop your skills and knowledge

signals.text: Relevant work experience (placements, insight programmes, internships) is viewed favourably and often feeds later hiring.

sources.quote: Relevant work experience is a good way of demonstrating a genuine interest in computing and is regarded favourably by employers.
Many employers run insight programmes, and especially spring weeks, with a view to hiring future interns and graduates.

actions.title: Build and ship a tool for a real group you belong to
actions.description: Find a manual process in a society, sports club or part-time job and replace it with a small web app that people actually use. Keep it running.
actions.evidence: Live link + public GitHub repo; README states the problem, stack, who uses it and one outcome (e.g. users, time saved), honestly measured.

sources.quote: You could look at sports clubs, groups and societies you already belong to and see if they have any processes or databases you could improve

actions.title: Take a tutorial project and make it genuinely yours
actions.description: Extend a course or tutorial project with a feature the tutorial did not cover, then add automated tests and a CI pipeline.
actions.evidence: Repo with passing CI; README section 'What I changed from the tutorial and why' (addresses SWE-17a: unextended tutorial clones).

sources.quote: If you were self-taught, then yes! Or if you’ve used that skill to solve a problem, yes again!

actions.title: Write a design note for your best project
actions.description: One page covering the architecture, two alternatives you rejected and why, known limitations, and what you would do with more time. Rehearse explaining it in 3 minutes.
actions.evidence: DESIGN.md in the repo, linked from the README.

sources.quote: you should expect to justify key decisions in your solution and describe what you’d have done differently with more time.

actions.title: Implement and benchmark core data structures and algorithms
actions.description: Implement several classic structures (e.g. hash map, heap, graph search), test them, and benchmark them against the standard library on growing inputs.
actions.evidence: Repo with tests and a README results table and chart; short write-up of what surprised you.

sources.quote: a logical, analytical and creative approach to problems and problem solving

actions.title: Team build with real code review
actions.description: Build something with 2-3 peers using issues, branches, pull requests and reviews, with a short planning cadence. Each person owns a clear part.
actions.evidence: Public repo showing PR history and reviews; README lists who built what (SWE-05: your own contribution).

sources.quote: the collaboration and project delivery skills we explore in this stage are just as important as technical excellence.

actions.title: CS50x (Harvard OpenCourseWare)
actions.description: Broad CS foundation (C, Python, SQL, web) ending in a final project. Signal value: the certificate on its own is low; the final project is what counts as evidence.

sources.quote: The main focus is on building single page applications with ReactJS that use REST APIs built with Node.js.

actions.description: University-level algorithms and data structures with problem sets. Learning value for technical interviews; signal value on a CV low.

sources.quote: Freely sharing knowledge with learners and educators around the world.

yearGuidance.1st: Ship 1-2 small projects with a README and GitHub link, go to a hackathon, apply to insight/spring programmes (many are aimed at first years).

actions.title: Question-led analysis of a public UK dataset
actions.description: Pick one concrete question, use a public open dataset, document cleaning decisions, choose a method, and end with a recommendation and its limitations.
actions.evidence: GitHub repo + README in four parts (question, cleaning, method, result) with one key chart; states dataset source and size (DAT-03).

sources.quote: Show how you defined a question, cleaned the data, chose an analytical method and communicated the result.

actions.title: Dashboard for a society or charity
actions.description: Turn a society's or charity's spreadsheets (members, events, donations) into a dashboard they can use for a real decision.
actions.evidence: Published dashboard link or screenshots + one paragraph on what it was used for, if anything (DAT-05 'so what'); do not claim an impact you did not observe.

sources.quote: You could also volunteer for a charity or community group that needs help organising, analysing or presenting data.

actions.title: Kaggle 'Getting Started' competition with an honest baseline
actions.description: Enter a Getting Started competition, report a simple baseline first, then your improved model and what drove the gain. Use it to learn; do not make Titanic-type data your headline project (DAT-11c).
actions.evidence: Public notebook with baseline vs final metric and leaderboard position.

sources.quote: Competitions with approachable ML fundamentals.

actions.title: Hypothesis-test or regression write-up
actions.description: Answer a question with a stated hypothesis, an appropriate test or regression, assumptions checked, and an effect size in plain English.

sources.quote: analytical and numerical ability to interpret large datasets and test conclusions

actions.title: SQL question bank on a real schema
actions.description: Load a public dataset into PostgreSQL, write a set of business questions and answer each with a query (joins, aggregates, window functions).
actions.evidence: Repo with schema, queries and a results table per question.

sources.quote: programming or query skills in SQL and, for some roles, Python or R

sources.quote: You can also get in touch with potential academic supervisors to ask for work shadowing opportunities.
